An extended warranty has a certain price and a conditional benefit: chart both

Use a three-state probability model, owner-cost bars, a cost bridge and sensitivity charts to separate repair risk, eligible claims and the cash a contract can save.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare the contract price with the repair exposure it actually removes

Interactive planning lab

Expected repair cost without the extra contract$320
Expected total owner cost with the extra contract$360
Expected extra owner cost with the contract; negative means lower$40

Original single-event illustration, with hypothetical nominal CAD amounts and assumed probabilities for one common comparison window. There are three mutually exclusive states: no repair, one eligible repair or one excluded repair. At most one event is modeled. Eligibility is conditional on that event occurring; it is not an observed approval rate or a promise about a particular claim. For an eligible event the provider pays the smaller of the cap and the positive repair cost less the deductible; otherwise it pays zero. The contract price is paid once at the start and never refunded. The same repair price is used for eligible and excluded events. Totals ignore discounting, financing, taxes beyond entered all-in amounts, shipping, downtime, multiple failures, repair-versus-replacement choices, depreciation and claim delays. Existing manufacturer, legal and card protection are outside the numerical comparison and must be reviewed before assigning any extra benefit to the purchased contract. Cost equality occurs at a whole-window event probability of 51.43%, holding eligibility, repair size, deductible and cap fixed.

The central idea

Expected repair cost, a payable benefit and the cash needed in an actual failure are three different amounts. A contract price buys only the protection its terms actually add.

01

Start with the protection window and the protection you already have

A checkout offer can make an extended warranty sound like a simple comparison between a small price now and a large repair later. The useful comparison is more specific: which repair, during which period, under which conditions, and how much of that repair would this extra contract actually fund?

The Government of Canada’s warranty guide distinguishes included manufacturer protection from extra-cost extended coverage and asks consumers to review terms, repair costs and possible credit-card overlap. A purchased contract should therefore be evaluated for its additional protection rather than credited with every repair benefit associated with owning the product.

This tool uses one common comparison window and a deliberately simplified event structure. There is either no modeled repair, one eligible repair, or one excluded repair. A repair has the same entered cost in the two repair states. The product purchase price is common to both alternatives and excluded. Existing legal, manufacturer and card protection are outside the calculation; the example does not decide anyone’s rights or whether a claim meets a real contract.

02

Separate the chance of a repair from the chance that a repair is eligible

The default repair-event probability is an assumed 40% over the entire comparison window. The assumed eligible share is 70% of those repair events. Multiplying them gives a 28% eligible-event probability. The excluded-event probability is 40% × 30%, or 12%, and the no-repair probability is 60%.

These are original teaching inputs, not a product failure study, a claim-approval statistic or an annual risk estimate. A different window, product age or definition of an eligible event would need its own evidence and assumptions. The model does not automatically convert a multi-year event probability into an annual rate.

The first chart keeps the denominator visible. “70% eligible” refers to the repair branch, not to every product bought. Treating it as a 70% chance of receiving a payment would confuse a conditional share with the overall probability. Even an eligible event can produce a zero payment if the deductible absorbs the entire repair cost.

03

Apply the deductible and payment cap before valuing the contract

The example repair costs CAD 800. The owner deductible is CAD 50, leaving CAD 750 before the cap. The provider-payment cap is CAD 500, so the modeled payment is CAD 500, not CAD 750 and not the full CAD 800. The owner retains CAD 300 of repair cost even in the eligible state.

The precise convention matters. This illustration defines the cap as a maximum provider payment after subtracting the deductible: payment = min(cap, max(0, repair cost − deductible)). It does not model a policy that first caps eligible repair charges and then subtracts a deductible. Read an actual contract before using either interpretation.

Raising the entered cap beyond CAD 750 cannot increase the default eligible payment because there is no more modeled eligible cost left to fund. Likewise, if the deductible reaches or exceeds the repair cost, the modeled payment becomes zero. A large number printed as a limit is not automatically a large economic benefit.

04

Keep the upfront price in every outcome

The contract costs CAD 180 at the start, with no refund in this illustration. If no repair occurs, the owner pays zero repair cost without the extra contract and CAD 180 with it. In the eligible repair state, the comparison is CAD 800 without the contract versus CAD 480 with it: CAD 180 plus the CAD 300 repair remainder.

In the excluded repair state, the owner pays CAD 800 without the contract and CAD 980 with it. The extra contract has not removed that repair exposure, and its initial price has already been spent. These bars show total nominal owner cost over the comparison window, not an estimate of an average bill.

They also do not show peak cash needed. A provider that reimburses later can leave the owner paying a larger invoice first. Repair timing, claims processing, downtime and shipping are excluded from the arithmetic. Those operational terms need a separate cash-access review even when a final payment is expected.

05

Reconcile the expected cost without turning it into a reserve target

Without the contract, expected repair cost is 40% × CAD 800, or CAD 320. The expected provider payment is 40% × 70% × CAD 500, or CAD 140. Expected owner cost with the contract is therefore CAD 180 + CAD 320 − CAD 140 = CAD 360, which is CAD 40 higher than the no-contract expected cost.

The waterfall makes the certain price and the contingent payment separate steps. A CAD 140 expected provider payment does not mean the provider pays CAD 140 when a repair occurs. In this restricted model, it pays either zero or CAD 500. Likewise, setting aside CAD 320 does not fully fund the possible CAD 800 repair.

Expected cost is one comparison, not a complete decision rule. A household may value reducing a particular cash exposure, convenience or service support, but those features need evidence in the actual offer. The tool places no dollar value on them and does not identify a contract that should be purchased.

06

Read the crossover as an assumption threshold, not a reliability estimate

Let W be the upfront contract price, p the whole-window repair probability, q the eligible share and P the provider payment in an eligible event. Expected extra owner cost is W − p × q × P. If qP is positive, cost equality occurs at p = W ÷ (qP).

At the defaults, CAD 180 ÷ (70% × CAD 500) gives about 51.43%. That threshold is above the selected 40% assumption. It does not show that the product’s actual repair probability is 51.43%, and it is not evidence for moving the probability input to make an offer look attractive.

A threshold above 100% cannot be reached within this single-event model. If no provider payment is available, a positive contract price cannot be recovered through modeled payments at any event probability. A zero-price, zero-payment contract ties the repair-cost baseline at every probability. These boundary cases are stated explicitly beside the charts.

07

Use the charts to ask better questions about the offer

  1. Define the comparison period and remove benefits already provided by other protection.
  2. Read the deductible, payment limit, eligible repairs and claim process in the actual terms.
  3. Keep the failure probability and conditional eligibility assumption separate.
  4. Compare the actual failure-state cash with the probability-weighted average.
  5. Test a lower eligible share and a smaller payment cap before interpreting the crossover.

The matrix changes eligibility and the payment cap while holding the selected repair probability fixed. Its signed cells report extra expected owner cost, so a negative value means lower modeled cost with the contract. It is not a product rating or a probability forecast. Multiple repairs, replacement instead of repair, depreciation, financing and the opportunity cost of the upfront price require a fuller model.
